```{python}
#| label: functions
#| include: false

def r_isco(a):
    """ISCO radius for signed spin a_*, in units of r_S (as in lecture 2)."""
    a = np.asarray(a, float)
    Z1 = 1.0 + np.cbrt(1.0 - a**2) * (np.cbrt(1.0 + a) + np.cbrt(1.0 - a))
    Z2 = np.sqrt(3.0 * a**2 + Z1**2)
    root = np.sqrt(np.clip((3.0 - Z1) * (3.0 + Z1 + 2.0 * Z2), 0.0, None))
    sign = -np.sign(a)
    return (3.0 + Z2 + sign * root) / 2.0


def efficiency(r):
    """Radiative efficiency for gas radiating down to r = r_ISCO, r in r_S."""
    return 1.0 - np.sqrt(1.0 - 1.0 / (3.0 * np.asarray(r, float)))
```

Last time we asked what the gas around a black hole *looks* like. This time we
ask how much energy it gives up on the way in. The answer turns out to be the
reason black holes are the brightest steady sources of light in the universe,
and the whole lecture is built on one idea: **every source of energy releases
some fraction of the rest mass of what it uses up, and that fraction is what
separates a campfire from a star from a quasar.**

## Rest mass is the currency

In [lecture 3](../special-relativity/index.qmd#e-mc2) we found that a mass $m$
at rest carries an energy $E_0 = mc^2$. Nothing that releases energy ever gets
all of it out. What it does is convert some fraction of the rest mass into
energy of some other kind — heat, light, motion — and leave the rest behind as
mass. For us, the part that matters is the energy that comes out as
**radiation**, because light is the only way we learn anything about a black
hole or a star from this far away. So call the fraction of the rest mass
energy that comes out as radiation the **efficiency**, $\eta$:

$$
E = \eta\, m c^2 .
$$ {#eq-efficiency}

The efficiency is a pure number between 0 and 1, and it is the single most
useful way to compare one power source with another, because it does not care
how much fuel there is.

**Hydrogen fusion**, which powers the Sun, turns four hydrogen nuclei into one
helium nucleus. The helium weighs a little less than the four hydrogen nuclei
did, and that missing mass is what comes out as energy: about 0.7% of it, so

$$
\eta_{\mathrm{fusion}} \approx 0.007 .
$$ {#eq-fusion}

That sounds small, and by the standards of this lecture it is. But fusion needs
something black holes cannot offer: a place for the fuel to sit and burn. Gas
falling into a black hole does not pile up on a surface. It crosses the horizon
and is gone, so a black hole gets essentially **nothing** from fusion. What it
has instead is gravity.

:::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: how much hydrogen does the Sun burn each second?"}
**The question.** The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium at an efficiency of 0.7%.
How many metric tons of hydrogen does it use up every second?

The Sun's luminosity is $L_\odot = 3.83 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$.
That is the energy it gives off per second, so by @eq-efficiency it is also
$\eta c^2$ times the mass of hydrogen it uses up per second.

**First, how much mass disappears each second.** Every erg that comes out was
once mass, so the rate at which mass is converted is $L_\odot/c^2$. Substitute
with the units attached and do no arithmetic yet:

$$
\frac{L_\odot}{c^2}
  = \frac{3.83 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}}
         {\left(3.00 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)^2}
$$

An erg is $\mathrm{g\,cm^2\,s^{-2}}$, so the top is
$\mathrm{g\,cm^2\,s^{-3}}$ and the bottom is $\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-2}}$. The
square centimeters cancel and one power of the seconds cancels, leaving
$\mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}$. *Do the units make sense?* We asked for a mass per
second, and that is what we have, so yes.

$$
\frac{L_\odot}{c^2} = 4.26 \times 10^{12}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}
$$

**Then, how much hydrogen that took.** Only 0.7% of the hydrogen's mass
became energy, so the hydrogen used up is larger by a factor of
$1/\eta_{\mathrm{fusion}}$:

$$
\dot m_{\mathrm{H}} = \frac{4.26 \times 10^{12}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}}{0.007}
  = 6.09 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}
$$

**Last, in metric tons.** Write each equivalence as a fraction, arranged so
that the unit you want to get rid of cancels. If you put a fraction the wrong
way up, nothing cancels and you can see it at once — so you never have to
remember whether to multiply or divide:

$$
6.09 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}
  \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{kg}}{10^{3}\ \mathrm{g}}
  \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{t}}{10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg}}
  = 6.09 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{t\,s^{-1}}
$$

Six hundred million tons of hydrogen every second — and the Sun has enough to
keep this up for about ten billion years.
::::

## Falling releases energy

Drop a ball and it speeds up. The energy it gains in motion came from its
gravitational potential energy, and when it hits the floor that energy turns
into heat and sound. Gas falling toward a black hole does the same thing, with
one important difference: it almost never falls straight in.

Gas arriving from far away nearly always has some sideways motion, so it goes
into **orbit**. Streams of orbiting gas collide, rub against one another and
settle into a thin, flat **accretion disk**. Friction inside the disk slowly
robs each bit of gas of energy, so it moves inward from one circular orbit to a
slightly smaller one, and the energy it loses is turned into heat and radiated
away. That is where the light comes from.

So the question is: how much energy has a bit of gas given up by the time it
has spiraled in to a circular orbit at radius $r$? For a circular orbit in
Newtonian gravity, the total energy — kinetic plus potential — is

$$
E_{\mathrm{orbit}} = -\frac{GMm}{2r} .
$$ {#eq-orbit}

Gas that started far away, essentially at rest, had a total energy of zero.
Every bit of the difference has been radiated, so the energy released is
$GMm/2r$. Now write it in terms of the Schwarzschild radius,
$r_S = 2GM/c^2$, which means $GM = r_S c^2/2$:

$$
\Delta E = \frac{GMm}{2r} = \frac{1}{4}\,\frac{r_S}{r}\,mc^2 .
$$ {#eq-newton-fraction}

Compare that with @eq-efficiency. The Newtonian efficiency of falling in to
radius $r$ is $\tfrac14\, r_S/r$, and **the mass of the black hole has
canceled**: all that matters is how close the gas gets *in units of $r_S$*,
exactly as it was for everything in [lecture 5](../strong-gravity/index.qmd).
A ten-solar-mass black hole and a billion-solar-mass one are equally good
engines, gram for gram.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about where the other half of the potential energy goes"}
Falling from far away to radius $r$, the gas loses $GMm/r$ of potential energy.
But @eq-newton-fraction says it radiates only half of that, $GMm/2r$.

The other half goes into **orbital motion**. A circular orbit at radius $r$
has speed $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, so its kinetic energy is
$\tfrac12 mv^2 = GMm/2r$ — exactly the half that was not radiated. The closer
in the gas gets, the faster it has to move to stay in orbit, and half of what
it gains by falling is spent keeping up.
:::

A disk turns a steady stream of gas into a steady output of light. Write the
amount of mass flowing in per unit time as $dM/dt$. Since time derivatives are
so common in physics, we frequently write $dM/dt$ as $\dot M$ to save space,
ink and time. This is known as the **accretion rate**. The luminosity — energy
per unit time — of gas that radiates all the way in to radius $r$ is then

$$
L = \frac{GM\dot M}{2r} .
$$ {#eq-lacc-newton}

**How good is this?** If the gas reaches $3\,r_S$ before it plunges in,
@eq-newton-fraction gives $\tfrac14 \times \tfrac13 = 8.3\%$ of the rest mass
— about twelve times better than fusion.

But look at what @eq-newton-fraction does if the gas keeps going. At
$r = r_S/4$ it says **100%** of the rest mass comes out, and inside that, more
than 100%. That cannot be right, and it is Newtonian gravity telling us it has
been pushed too close to a black hole.

## Where falling stops paying: the ISCO

::: {.panel-tabset .tracks}

### Physical intuition

The major criterion for radiative efficiency is spin, and the reason is the
innermost stable circular orbit from
[lecture 2](../spinning-bhs-and-tidal/index.qmd#the-isco).

Gas in the disk radiates as it spirals slowly inward from one circular orbit to
the next. That works only as long as there *is* a next circular orbit to move
to. Inside $r_{\mathrm{ISCO}}$ there is none: the gas stops spiraling and
plunges, reaching the horizon in about the time it takes to go once around,
with no time to shed its energy as light. So **the energy that comes out is
the energy the gas has given up by the time it reaches the ISCO**, and nothing
after.

That is why spin matters so much. The bigger $a_*$ is, the smaller the ISCO
radius is, and therefore the more radiation can escape before the matter
plunges in. It is also why the gas at the inner edge of the disk is moving so
fast — at a non-spinning black hole's ISCO it moves at exactly half the speed
of light, as we found in [lecture 6](../seeing-black-holes/index.qmd).

### Mathematical explanation

Close to a black hole we have to use general relativity rather than Newton, but
the idea is the same: the efficiency is the fraction of rest mass energy the gas
has lost by the time it reaches the ISCO. Write the energy of the gas at the
ISCO as a fraction $E$ of its rest mass energy. Then

$$
\eta = 1 - E .
$$ {#eq-eta-def}

The relation between spin and that energy comes out of the Kerr solution, and
it is not pretty:

$$
a_* = \frac{4\sqrt{2}\,(1 - E^2)^{1/2} - 2E}{3\sqrt{3}\,(1 - E^2)} ,
$$ {#eq-spin-energy}

where, as with the ISCO formula in lecture 2, a positive $a_*$ means gas orbiting the
same way the black hole spins and a negative one means the opposite way. The
formula carries that sign by itself.

There is a much friendlier form if you already know $r_{\mathrm{ISCO}}$. At the
ISCO, and **only** at the ISCO, the efficiency is

$$
\eta = 1 - \sqrt{1 - \frac{r_S}{3\,r_{\mathrm{ISCO}}}} .
$$ {#eq-eta-isco}

Once again it depends only on a radius in units of $r_S$, so once again the
mass cancels. Put in the three values of $r_{\mathrm{ISCO}}$ from lecture 2:

| spin | $r_{\mathrm{ISCO}}$ | $\eta$, general relativity | $\tfrac14 r_S/r_{\mathrm{ISCO}}$, Newton |
|---|---|---|---|
| $a_* = -1$ | $4.5\,r_S$ | $1 - \sqrt{25/27} = 3.8\%$ | 5.6% |
| $a_* = 0$ | $3\,r_S$ | $1 - \sqrt{8/9} = 5.7\%$ | 8.3% |
| $a_* = +1$ | $0.5\,r_S$ | $1 - \sqrt{1/3} = 42\%$ | 50% |

**Newton overestimates at every spin** — by about half for a non-spinning black
hole — so the true numbers are the ones in the general-relativity column. But
even the smallest of them is five times better than fusion, and a maximally
spinning black hole turns 42% of the rest mass of what falls into it into
light.[These are the classic thin-disk values, worked out by Novikov and Thorne
[-@novikov1973] using the orbits of @bardeen1972.]{.aside
.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Numerical exploration

Here are lecture 2's ISCO formula and @eq-eta-isco working together across the
range of spins, with the Newtonian estimate and a comparison with fusion
alongside.

```{python}
#| label: eta-ladder

import numpy as np


def r_isco_over_rs(a):
    """ISCO radius for signed spin a_*, in units of r_S."""
    Z1 = 1.0 + np.cbrt(1.0 - a**2) * (np.cbrt(1.0 + a) + np.cbrt(1.0 - a))
    Z2 = np.sqrt(3.0 * a**2 + Z1**2)
    root = np.sqrt(max((3.0 - Z1) * (3.0 + Z1 + 2.0 * Z2), 0.0))
    sign = -np.sign(a)
    return (3.0 + Z2 + sign * root) / 2.0


def efficiency(r):
    """Radiative efficiency for gas radiating down to r = r_ISCO, r in r_S."""
    return 1.0 - np.sqrt(1.0 - 1.0 / (3.0 * r))


spins = [-1.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.998, 1.0]

print("    a*     r_ISCO     GR eta   Newton   vs fusion")
for a in spins:
    r = r_isco_over_rs(a)
    eta = efficiency(r)
    print(f"{a:+6.3f}  {r:5.3f} r_S   {100 * eta:5.2f}%   {25 / r:5.2f}%   {eta / 0.007:5.1f}x")
```

## The luminosity of accretion

Now we can say how bright an accreting black hole is. Let's consider how much
matter per unit time is flowing in toward the black hole: $\dot M$. Some
fraction of that mass-energy is turned into radiative energy, and we have been
calling that fraction $\eta$. For every bit of mass $M$ that is accreted onto
the black hole, an amount of energy $E = \eta M c^2$ is released. Since we are
interested in the amount of energy per unit time ($L = \dot E$), we use the
amount of mass per unit time:

$$
L_{\mathrm{acc}} = \eta\, \dot M c^2 .
$$ {#eq-lacc}

We call $\eta$ the **radiative efficiency** because it tells us how much of the
mass gets turned into radiation. Typical values run from about 0.06 for a black
hole that is not spinning to 0.42 for one that is spinning as fast as it can;
0.1 is the round number astronomers reach for when they do not know the spin.

:::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: a black hole eating one Sun a year"}
**The question.** What is the luminosity, in units of the Sun's luminosity, of
a black hole accreting one solar mass of gas per year at the standard
radiative efficiency of 10%?

So $\dot M = 1\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ and $\eta = 0.1$. First turn the
accretion rate into grams per second, with each equivalence written as a
fraction so that the unwanted unit cancels:

$$
\dot M = \frac{1\,M_\odot}{1\ \mathrm{yr}}
  \times \frac{1.99 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}}{1\,M_\odot}
  \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{yr}}{3.156 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}}
  = 6.30 \times 10^{25}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}
$$

Now substitute into @eq-lacc with the units attached:

$$
L_{\mathrm{acc}} = 0.1 \times 6.30 \times 10^{25}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}
  \times \left(3.00 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)^2
$$

The units are $\mathrm{g\,s^{-1}} \times \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-2}} =
\mathrm{g\,cm^2\,s^{-3}}$, which is an erg per second. *Do the units make
sense?* A luminosity is an energy per second, so yes.

$$
L_{\mathrm{acc}} = 5.67 \times 10^{45}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}
  \times \frac{1\,L_\odot}{3.83 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}}
  = 1.48 \times 10^{12}\,L_\odot
$$

A trillion Suns, from one Sun's worth of gas a year. That is roughly what a
bright quasar does.
::::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## Luminosity and flux

Two different quantities both get called "how bright", and it matters which is
which. The **luminosity** $L$ is the total energy a source emits per second, in
$\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. It belongs to the source: the Sun's luminosity is the
same whether you are standing next to it or looking at it from another galaxy.

The **flux** $F$ is how much of that energy passes through each square
centimeter of a surface per second, in $\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$. It
depends on where you are. A source that shines equally in all directions
spreads its light over a sphere, and at a distance $d$ that sphere has area
$4\pi d^2$, so

$$
F = \frac{L}{4\pi d^2} .
$$ {#eq-flux}

This is the inverse-square law: twice as far away, a quarter the flux. At the
Earth, $1\ \mathrm{AU}$ from the Sun, it gives
$F = 1.36 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$ — about the power of a
hair dryer landing on every square meter of ground facing the Sun.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-flux}

1. Imagine a star *exactly* like the Sun, $100\ \mathrm{AU}$ from Earth. What
   would we measure its luminosity to be? What would we measure its flux to
   be?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   Its luminosity is the Sun's, $3.83 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ —
   luminosity does not depend on distance. Its flux is
   $136\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$, ten thousand times less than the
   Sun's at 1 AU.
   :::

:::

## Blackbody radiation and effective temperature

We now know how much energy accreting gas gives off. What does that light look
like? The simplest answer, and a surprisingly good one, is that hot gas glows
like a **blackbody**: an idealized object that absorbs all light falling on it
and emits light whose spectrum depends on nothing but its temperature.

```{python}
#| label: fig-blackbody
#| fig-cap: "Blackbody spectra at four temperatures. The curves are nested: a hotter blackbody is brighter at every wavelength, and its peak moves to shorter, bluer wavelengths. The dashed line follows the peak. The shaded band is visible light."
#| fig-alt: "A graph of blackbody intensity, in arbitrary units, against wavelength from zero to three micrometers. Four smooth, single-peaked curves are drawn for temperatures of 3000, 4000, 5000 and 6000 kelvin. Each hotter curve lies entirely above each cooler one. The 6000 kelvin curve is tallest, with its peak near half a micrometer inside the shaded band of visible light; the peaks of the cooler curves are lower and farther to the right, with the 3000 kelvin peak near one micrometer, in the infrared. A dashed line connects the four peaks, sloping down and to the right."
#| fig-height: 4.03

h, c, k = 6.6262e-27, 2.99792456e10, 1.3806e-16   # the course constants sheet
wien = 0.289789                                     # cm K


def planck(lam_cm, T):
    """Blackbody intensity per unit wavelength, cgs."""
    return 2 * h * c**2 / lam_cm**5 / np.expm1(h * c / (lam_cm * k * T))


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.03))

lam_um = np.linspace(0.05, 3.0, 3000)
temps = [6000, 5000, 4000, 3000]
norm = planck(wien / 6000, 6000)

ax.axvspan(0.38, 0.75, color=GRID, zorder=0)
ax.annotate("visible", xy=(0.565, 1.04), ha="center", color=MUTED, fontsize=10)

peaks_x, peaks_y = [], []
for T in temps:
    y = planck(lam_um * 1e-4, T) / norm
    ax.plot(lam_um, y, color=BLUE, zorder=3)
    xp = wien / T * 1e4
    yp = planck(wien / T, T) / norm
    peaks_x.append(xp)
    peaks_y.append(yp)
    ax.annotate(f"{T} K", xy=(xp, yp), xytext=(10, 4),
                textcoords="offset points", color=INK2, fontsize=10)

tt = np.linspace(2900, 6100, 200)
ax.plot(wien / tt * 1e4, planck(wien / tt, tt) / norm, color=MUTED,
        linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2, zorder=2)
ax.plot(peaks_x, peaks_y, marker="o", color=ORANGE, markeredgecolor=SURFACE,
        markeredgewidth=1.2, linestyle="none", zorder=4)

ax.set_xlabel(r"wavelength $\lambda$  ($\mathrm{\mu m}$)")
ax.set_ylabel("intensity  (arbitrary units)")
ax.set_xlim(0.0, 3.0)
ax.set_ylim(0.0, 1.12)
plt.show()
```

The spectrum of a blackbody, the intensity of light at each wavelength, is

$$
B_\lambda(T) = \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5}\,
  \frac{1}{\exp\left(hc/\lambda k T\right) - 1}
  \qquad \left[\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}\,\text{Å}^{-1}}\right] ,
$$ {#eq-planck}

where $h$ is Planck's constant and $k$ is Boltzmann's. You will not need to
calculate with @eq-planck in this course, but two things about its shape,
both visible in @fig-blackbody, you will use all the time:

- **The curves are nested.** A hotter blackbody has more area under its curve,
  and more flux at every wavelength.
- **Hotter means a higher-energy peak: bluer.** The wavelength of the peak is
  inversely proportional to the temperature, $\lambda_{\max} T = 0.29\
  \mathrm{cm\,K}$, so doubling the temperature halves the peak wavelength.

So now that we are reminded of that, we can think about stars as spherical
blackbody radiators. Stars have *surface* temperatures of 3000 K to
100,000 K. Every square centimeter of a blackbody's surface emits a flux
$\sigma T^4$, where $\sigma$ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, and a sphere of
radius $R$ has $4\pi R^2$ of them. So we can calculate a star's luminosity
knowing only its temperature and radius:

$$
L_{\mathrm{BB}} = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4 .
$$ {#eq-stefan}

It also works the other way round. For an object with a known luminosity and
radius, we can calculate its **effective temperature**, $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$, by
assuming that it is a blackbody with the same radius and luminosity. Nothing
promises the object really is a blackbody — which is why it is called
*effective* — but it is almost always the first number an astronomer works out.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

   luminosity and radius on the constants sheet.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   About 5770 K.

   times larger. Is it more or less luminous than the Sun? By what factor?

## Summary

| Quantity | Expression | What to remember |
|---|---|---|
| Efficiency | $E = \eta\, mc^2$ | The fraction of rest mass that comes out as energy |
| Fusion | $\eta \approx 0.007$ | Needs a surface to burn on, so black holes get none of it |
| Newtonian release | $\Delta E = \tfrac14\,(r_S/r)\,mc^2$ | Half the potential energy; the mass of the black hole cancels |
| ISCO efficiency | $\eta = 1 - \sqrt{1 - r_S/3r_{\mathrm{ISCO}}}$ | 3.8% retrograde, 5.7% non-spinning, 42% maximal spin. Newton overestimates |
| Accretion luminosity | $L_{\mathrm{acc}} = \eta\, \dot M c^2$ | $\eta \approx 0.1$ when the spin is unknown |
| Flux | $F = L/4\pi d^2$ | Luminosity belongs to the source; flux depends on where you stand |
| Blackbody | $L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$ | Hotter is brighter at every wavelength, and bluer |
| Effective temperature | from $L$ and $R$ | The temperature of a blackbody with the same size and luminosity |

Accretion onto a black hole is the most efficient way we know of to turn mass
into light. That raises an obvious question: if you pour gas in faster and
faster, does the black hole just get brighter and brighter without limit? Next
time we will find that it cannot, because the light it makes pushes back on the
gas trying to fall in.
